name: Fragmentarian spiritual individualism
title: Fragmentarian spiritual individualism | Takuya Nemoto
description: A framework that treats life, faith, society, ideas and eschatology as self-contained fragments rather than one continuous story, and asks how to inhabit fragmentation with rigor. A preprint, not peer-reviewed.
taglineHtml: Fragmentation is not a wound to be repaired. The framework asks how to inhabit it with discipline. It has not been peer-reviewed.

blocks.title: The framework, its limited metaphors, and the limits it keeps
blocks.html:
Fragmentarian Spiritual Individualism treats life, faith, society, ideas and eschatology as self-contained fragments rather than as one continuous story. It was set out in the paper “Fragmentarian Spiritual Individualism” (August 2026; 10.5281/zenodo.22064241). It is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed.

Fragmentation is not treated as a wound. Therapeutic, communitarian and liberal-humanist traditions alike treat fragmentation as a wound to be cured: recover a coherent life story, re-embed the person in a community, or restore rational self-governance. The paper goes the other way. Fragmentation may be a more accurate description of how a life is actually lived. The task is then

… not to overcome fragmentation but to inhabit it with rigor.

Four things share one flaw. Modern rationalism, institutional religion, narrative selfhood and capitalist self-realization each subordinate the singular, discontinuous individual to an external logic of continuity: bureaucratic, doctrinal, biographical or economic.

The framework is built from six fragments. Tactical solitude (Kierkegaard’s single individual, the zanshin of Bushido). Institutional detachment in faith (Eckhart’s Gelassenheit, Boehme’s Ungrund). The fusion of ideas and discipline (bun-bu-ryōdō, Musashi’s Book of Five Rings, Hadot’s spiritual exercises). An aesthetics of form and ritual against efficiency (kata, set against Marx’s alienation and Weber’s iron cage). An eschatology of finitude (Heidegger’s being-toward-death, an academic reading of Hagakure). A genealogy of its own sources (Yoshimoto Takaaki’s communal illusion, Karatani Kojin’s transcritique).

“Combat”, “death” and “glory” are limited to metaphor. Combat is not violence: the claim is not that philosophical reflection should be supplemented by interpersonal violence. Death is neither praised nor urged: it is not a valorization of dying, still less an exhortation toward it. Glory is a property much closer to craftsmanship than to domination: a fragment reaching formal completion.

The fragments are not merged into one system. Merging them would repeat, at the level of exposition, the demand for a continuous story that the framework rejects at the level of life. The method follows Karatani’s transcritique.

The limits are left unresolved. One is how radical autonomy relates to the claims of justice, care and reciprocity owed to others. The other is how an ontology of discontinuous fragments can support a discipline kept up over a whole life. The paper also notes that much of what circulates today as Bushido was systematized and idealized in the late Edo and Meiji periods, and uses it as a philosophical resource, not as a fixed tradition.

The record admits three things. The manuscript was written in Japanese, and the published English is a translation by a language model (E5). The author has not read most of the cited sources (E6). Nitobe Inazō, named in the text, is missing from the references (E9). All three are in the errata. The paper is frozen; corrections go into the errata.

This is not a theory. The paper describes its method as synthesis across traditions rather than systematic argument from first principles, offering conceptual resources rather than empirical validation. Claiming a contribution and having the field count it are different things.

The paper was drafted with Claude (Anthropic), and this page was written with Claude Code. The author is responsible for the claims. Claude is not an author.
